Culture

Culture, its components, cultural diversity and cultural competence in nursing care.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Define culture and list its components
  • Explain cultural relativism and ethnocentrism
  • Describe how culture affects health beliefs and care

In simple words

Culture is the shared beliefs, values, customs, language and way of life of a group of people. It is learned and passed from one generation to the next.

Culture affects what people eat, how they see illness, what treatment they accept, how they express pain and who makes decisions in the family.

Cultural competence means respecting and adapting care to each patient’s culture.

Components of culture

Component Meaning Health example
Beliefs Ideas accepted as true Belief that illness is punishment
Values Ideas of right and wrong Value of family decision-making
Customs Traditional practices Diet during illness or pregnancy
Language Way of communicating Patient may not speak the nurse’s language
Symbols Objects with meaning Religious symbols worn by patients

Ethnocentrism and cultural relativism

  • Ethnocentrism — judging another culture by your own standards (“my way is right”).
  • Cultural relativism — understanding a culture on its own terms.

Nurses must avoid ethnocentrism and respect the patient’s cultural beliefs, even when different from their own.

Culture and health

  • Food beliefs affect diet and recovery.
  • Some cultures prefer home remedies before hospital care.
  • Gender norms may affect who can examine the patient.
  • Pain expression varies — some cultures show pain openly, others hide it.

🔴 Cultural competence

Cultural competence is respecting and adapting care to each patient’s culture. Avoid judging another culture by your own standards.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Ask about beliefs — gently ask what the patient thinks caused the illness and what they expect from treatment.
  • Respect food customs — arrange suitable meals; fasting may matter for religious reasons.
  • Respect gender norms — offer a same-gender caregiver when possible for intimate care.
  • Use interpreters — if language differs, use a trained interpreter; do not rely on children.
  • Include the family — many cultures make health decisions as a family.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Culture is shared beliefs, values, customs, language and way of life, learned and passed on.
  2. Components include beliefs, values, customs, language and symbols.
  3. Ethnocentrism is judging another culture by your own standards.
  4. Cultural relativism means understanding a culture on its own terms.
  5. Culture affects diet, illness beliefs, pain expression and decision-making.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Cultural competence means adapting care to the patient’s culture.
  2. Some cultures prefer home remedies before hospital care.
  3. Use a trained interpreter when language differs.

📌 Memory trick

Culture parts: “B-V-C-L-S” — Beliefs, Values, Customs, Language, Symbols.

60-second revision

  • Culture = shared beliefs, values, customs, language, way of life.
  • Learned and passed across generations.
  • Components: beliefs, values, customs, language, symbols.
  • Ethnocentrism = judge by own standards; avoid it.
  • Cultural relativism = understand on its own terms.
  • Culture affects food, illness beliefs, pain, decisions.

Test yourself

Culture is:

Answer: B. Culture is learned and shared within a group, not inherited biologically.

Ethnocentrism means:

Answer: B. Ethnocentrism is believing your own culture is the standard by which others should be judged.

Cultural competence in nursing means:

Answer: B. Cultural competence means adapting care to respect each patient's cultural beliefs and practices.

Which is a component of culture?

Answer: B. Language is a component of culture; blood group, height and age are biological.

If a patient’s language differs from the nurse’s, the nurse should:

Answer: B. Use a trained interpreter for accurate communication; children are not suitable interpreters.
